Yes, for any commit that gets replayed. A commit's hash covers its tree, parent hash, author/committer info, timestamps, and message. Rebasing gives a commit a new parent, which changes the hash. Every descendant's parent hash then changes too, so all commits after the first rewritten one get new hashes.

Exceptions: commits already sitting on the new base are not rewritten (e.g., a fast-forward rebase, or commits at the start of the range that are unchanged). Git also skips commits whose patch is already upstream.

Consequence: don't rebase commits that others have pulled, or you'll force them to reconcile diverged history.
